What this gives a session: after Claude edits a .go, .rs, .py or .vue file, Claude Code sends the buffer to `shared/tools/nx-polyglot-graph/lsp.mjs` and puts what comes back into the conversation. So a layer-, scope- or licence-violating import in those languages is caught at the edit, by the same `module-boundaries.config.mjs` table ESLint reads — instead of surviving until CI, or surviving CI, which today it does: `@nx/enforce-module-boundaries` reads only JS and TS, so a Go project's tags have no mechanism behind them and its `lint` target exits 0 over a violating import.

Why those four extensions and not .ts: ESLint already enforces the same table on JS and TS in this workspace, and Claude Code gives ONE server per extension — the first registered wins and the rest never start. Claiming .ts here would silently displace whichever TypeScript server the developer actually needs, to re-answer a question that is already answered. The four claimed extensions are exactly the languages that have no enforcement today, and `src/lsp/editor-config.integration.test.mjs` in that project fails if this list and the analyzer registry ever disagree.

Node must be on PATH; nothing else is installed. Claude Code ignores manifest keys it does not know, which is where this note lives.

Bump `version` (here and in the marketplace entry, which must match) whenever THIS FILE changes — an installed plugin is cached per version, so an unbumped edit reaches nobody. Editing the server itself needs no bump: `args` points at the working tree, not at the cached copy.
name: nx-polyglot-graph
description: Module-boundary diagnostics for the languages ESLint cannot read: Go, Rust, Python and Vue
